claim: The striatum is involved in the acquisition and execution of action sequences.
source: The striatum is involved in the acquisition and execution of action sequences (Costa, 2011; Graybiel, 1998; Hikosaka et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The striatum has been linked to temporal information processing.
source: It has also been linked to temporal information processing (Bakhurin et al., 2017; Emmons et al., 2017; Gouvêa et al., 2015; Matell et al., 2003; Mello et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The striatum is linked to the use of temporal information for action initiation timing.
source: and to the use of temporal information for the action initiation timing (Kunimatsu et al., 2018; Thura and Cisek, 2017; Yau et al., 2020)⁠.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Well-learned action sequences may be difficult to withhold when triggering cues are present.
source: However, these actions may be difficult to withhold when triggering cues are present, and also difficult to stop once they have been initiated (Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Gillan et al., 2016a; Graybiel, 2008; Knowlton and Patterson, 2016; Robbins and Costa, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: In neuropsychiatric conditions involving malfunctioning of cortico-basal ganglia circuits, action sequences might be started at inappropriate contexts and timings.
source: Moreover, in neuropsychiatric conditions involving malfunctioning of cortico-basal ganglia circuits, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, Tourette syndrome, obsessive–compulsive disorder, and drug addiction (Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Gillan et al., 2016a; Singer, 2016) action sequences might be started at inappropriate contexts and timings.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: How the striatum contributes to action sequence initiation timing remains poorly understood.
source: However, how the striatum contributes to action sequence initiation timing remains poorly understood.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Impulsivity has been identified as a vulnerability factor for compulsive drug seeking habits.
source: Interestingly, impulsivity has been identified as a vulnerability factor for compulsive drug seeking habits (Belin and Everitt, 2008)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Recent studies link impulsivity to automaticity in behavior.
source: Recent studies link impulsivity to automaticity in behavior (Ersche et al., 2019; Gillan et al., 2016b; Hogarth et al., 2012)⁠
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claim: Impulsivity is linked to a preponderance of habitual over goal-directed behavioral control.
source: and a preponderance of habitual over goal-directed behavioral control (Everitt et al., 2008; Voon et al., 2015)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Dorsolateral striatal (DLS) circuits support habitual stimulus–response control whereas dorsomedial striatal (DMS) circuits mediate cognitive-based deliberative control.
source: An influential theory in the field postulates a dual control system for behavior, where dorsolateral striatal (DLS) circuits support habitual stimulus–response control whereas dorsomedial striatal (DMS) circuits mediate cognitive-based deliberative control (Balleine and Dickinson, 1998; Daw et al., 2005; Graybiel, 2008; Yin and Knowlton, 2006)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research describing an influential theory

claim: During action sequence learning, neuronal activity in the DLS rapidly evolves to mark the initiation and termination of the acquired sequence.
source: During action sequence learning, neuronal activity in the DLS rapidly evolves to mark the initiation and termination of the acquired sequence (Jin and Costa, 2010; Jog et al., 1999)⁠
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DLS activity possibly contributes to the release of action sequences as a behavioral unit or chunk.
source: , possibly contributing to its release as a behavioral unit or chunk (Graybiel, 2008)⁠.
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation

claim: The DMS encodes reward expectancy, reward prediction errors, and trial outcomes even after extensive training.
source: In contrast, the DMS encodes reward expectancy, reward prediction errors, and trial outcomes even after extensive training (Kim et al., 2009; Kubota et al., 2009; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Samejima et al., 2005; Thorn et al., 2010; Vandaele et al., 2019)⁠.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: DMS features likely contribute to the regulation of explore–exploit, cost–benefit, and speed–accuracy tradeoffs during decision making.
source: All these features likely contribute to the regulation of explore–exploit (Barnes et al., 2005)⁠, cost–benefit (Floresco et al., 2008; Schultz, 2015)⁠, and speed–accuracy (Thura and Cisek, 2017) tradeoffs during decision making.
evidence: Inference supported by citations to prior research

claim: A bias toward exploration and risk-taking may contribute to impulsivity traits.
source: A bias toward exploration and risk-taking (Addicott et al., 2017)⁠, low tolerance for delayed rewards (Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Monterosso and Ainslie, 1999; Wittmann and Paulus, 2008) and elevated internal urgency states (Carland et al., 2019)⁠, may all contribute to impulsivity traits.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Low tolerance for delayed rewards may contribute to impulsivity traits.
source: A bias toward exploration and risk-taking (Addicott et al., 2017)⁠, low tolerance for delayed rewards (Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Monterosso and Ainslie, 1999; Wittmann and Paulus, 2008) and elevated internal urgency states (Carland et al., 2019)⁠, may all contribute to impulsivity traits.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Elevated internal urgency states may contribute to impulsivity traits.
source: A bias toward exploration and risk-taking (Addicott et al., 2017)⁠, low tolerance for delayed rewards (Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Monterosso and Ainslie, 1999; Wittmann and Paulus, 2008) and elevated internal urgency states (Carland et al., 2019)⁠, may all contribute to impulsivity traits.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: How neuronal activity in the dorsal striatum informs about enhanced premature responding in conditions of high impulsivity remains unknown.
source: However, how neuronal activity in the dorsal striatum informs about enhanced premature responding in conditions of high impulsivity, remains unknown.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Rats were trained to withhold a rewarded action sequence until a waiting interval has elapsed.
source: Here, we studied striatal activity during a self-paced task where rats have to withhold a rewarded action sequence until a waiting interval has elapsed (Zold and Hussain Shuler, 2015)⁠.
evidence: Description of the experimental task used in this study

claim: Prematurely initiated sequences were penalized by re-initiating the waiting interval.
source: Prematurely initiated sequences were penalized by re-initiating the waiting interval.
evidence: Description of the experimental task design

claim: Animals showed premature responding even after extensive training.
source: Despite the negative effect this timer re-initialization may have, the animals showed premature responding even after extensive training.
evidence: Behavioral observation from the study

claim: Animals often failed to interrupt the execution of the action sequence although there was sensory evidence of its untimely initiation.
source: Moreover, they often failed to interrupt the execution of the action sequence although there was sensory evidence of its untimely initiation.
evidence: Behavioral observation from the study

claim: A peak of striatal activity preceding trial initiation was modulated by the time waited before responding.
source: We found a peak of striatal activity preceding trial initiation that was modulated by the time waited before responding.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding from the study

claim: The modulation of anticipatory striatal activity grew at a faster rate in adolescent rats.
source: In addition, this modulation grew at a faster rate in adolescent rats.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding comparing age groups

claim: Adolescent rats show a strong prevalence of impulsive responses compared to adults.
source: Interestingly, the modulation is steeper in adolescent rats, which show a strong prevalence of impulsive responses compared to adults.
evidence: Behavioral finding comparing age groups

claim: The anticipatory striatal activity reflects the animals' subjective reward expectation based on the elapsed waiting time.
source: We hypothesize this anticipatory striatal activity reflects the animals' subjective reward expectation, based on the elapsed waiting time
evidence: Authors' hypothesis based on their findings

claim: The steeper waiting modulation in adolescence reflects age-related differences in temporal discounting, internal urgency states, or explore–exploit balance.
source: while the steeper waiting modulation in adolescence reflects age-related differences in temporal discounting, internal urgency states, or explore–exploit balance.
evidence: Authors' hypothesis about the mechanism underlying age differences

claim: Water-deprived rats were trained to obtain water from a lick tube located within a nose-poke by emitting a sequence of eight licks following a visual cue.
source: Water-deprived rats were trained to obtain water from a lick tube located within a nose-poke by emitting a sequence of eight licks following a visual cue (Figure 1A, B; task modified from Zold and Hussain Shuler, 2015)⁠.
evidence: Description of experimental methods with reference to figures

claim: In timely trials initiated 2.5 s after the end of the previous trial, a 100-ms duration visual cue reported that there was a 0.5 probability of receiving a water reward.
source: In those trials initiated 2.5 s after the end of the previous trial (timely trials), a 100-ms duration visual cue (two symmetrical green LEDs located at the nose-poke sides) reported that there was a 0.5 probability of receiving a water reward.
evidence: Description of experimental task design

claim: Prematurely initiated trials (<2.5 s waiting time) were penalized by re-initiating the timer and had no visual cue associated with them.
source: In contrast, prematurely initiated trials (<2.5 s waiting time) were penalized by re-initiating the timer and had no visual cue associated with them.
evidence: Description of experimental task design

claim: Spike discharges and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded from the dorsal striatum using custom-made tetrodes.
source: Spike discharges and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded from the dorsal striatum using custom-made tetrodes (Vandecasteele et al., 2012)⁠ (representative localization Figure 1C, for detailed localization see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of experimental methods with reference to figures

claim: Adult rats learned to make timely nose-poke entries followed by an 8-lick sequence.
source: Adult rats learned to make timely nose-poke entries followed by an 8-lick sequence (Figure 1D).
evidence: Behavioral result with reference to figure

claim: There was a twofold increase in the reward rate in sessions late in training compared to early in training.
source: This was evidenced by a twofold increase in the reward rate in sessions late in training (after three consecutive sessions with >70% correct trials) compared to early in training (Figure 1E, P=6.10 × 10–5, Wilcoxon matched pairs test, n pairs = 15).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figure

claim: Performance in 8-lick trials became faster with training.
source: Performance in 8-lick trials became faster with training (Figure 1F–H): trial duration (learning stage: F(1, 14) = 19.85, p = 5.43 × 10−4, trial: F(1, 14) = 19.91, p = 5.37 × 10−4), latency to the first lick (learning stage: F(1, 14) = 12.59, p = 3.21 × 10−4), and time to complete the 8-lick sequence (learning stage: F(1, 14) = 18.33, p = 7.60 × 10−4), diminished with training for both rewarded and unrewarded timely trials (significant effect of learning stage, non-significant interaction, two-way Repeated Measures ANOVAs).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figures

claim: Premature nose-poke entries delayed the opportunity to get the reward as evidenced by a negative correlation between the relative number of premature trials and reward rate across sessions.
source: Premature nose-poke entries delayed the opportunity to get the reward as evidenced by a negative correlation between the relative number of premature trials and reward rate across sessions (Figure 2A, R2 = 0.090, F(1, 60) = 5.96, p = 0.018, n = 62 sessions from 5 rats).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figure

claim: Premature trials diminished with training from >30% of all trials at the beginning of training to ~15% at the end of training.
source: Premature trials diminished with training from >30% of all trials at the beginning of training to ~15% at the end of training.
evidence: Behavioral observation from the study

claim: Premature trials followed by an 8-lick sequence rose from 40% to 70% of all premature trials with training.
source: However, premature trials followed by an 8-lick sequence rose from 40% to 70% of all premature trials with training, paralleling the relative increase of 8-lick sequences observed in timely trials (Figure 2B, F(1, 14) = 32.87, p = 5.20 × 10−5 for learning stage and F(1, 14) = 121.74, p = 2.73 × 10−8 for trial timing, no interaction, two-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figure

claim: Behavior during premature trials was modified by learning, just like in timely trials.
source: These data suggest that behavior during premature trials was modified by learning, just like in timely trials.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral data

claim: Time to complete the 8-lick sequence diminished with training both for timely and premature trials.
source: Further supporting this presumption, time to complete the 8-lick sequence (F(1, 14) = 15.63, p = 0.001), latency to the first lick of the sequence (F(1, 14) = 14.30, p = 0.002) and variation coefficient of the inter-lick intervals (an index of the regularity of such intervals; F(1, 14) = 6.78, p = 0.021), diminished with training both for timely and premature trials (Figure 2C–E; significant effect of learning stage, no effect of trial type, no interaction, two-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figures

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the percentage of premature trials followed by an 8-lick sequence and reward rate.
source: Remarkably, even though premature trials were detrimental to reward rate (Figure 2A), there was a significant positive correlation between the percentage of premature trials followed by an 8-lick sequence and reward rate (Figure 2F, R2 = 0.478, F(1, 60) = 54.98, p = 1.03 × 10−9, n = 62 sessions from 5 rats).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figures

claim: The probability of a trial including an 8-lick sequence sharply increased at the end of the 2.5 s waiting interval, peaked immediately after its finalization, and then diminished gradually.
source: The probability of a trial including an 8-lick sequence sharply increased at the end of the 2.5 s waiting interval, peaked immediately after its finalization, and then diminished gradually.
evidence: Behavioral observation from the study

claim: Rats trained with a long waiting interval (5 s) quickly learned to adjust trial initiations to a shorter waiting interval (2.5 s).
source: Finally, rats trained with the long waiting interval (5 s) quickly learned to adjust trial initiations to a shorter waiting interval (2.5 s) (Figure 2I), suggesting that premature trials with 8-lick sequences served to adapt behavior to changes in the waiting time requirements of the task that otherwise would have passed unnoticed to the rats.
evidence: Behavioral observation with reference to figure and authors' interpretation

claim: Premature trials with 8-lick sequences served to adapt behavior to changes in the waiting time requirements of the task.
source: suggesting that premature trials with 8-lick sequences served to adapt behavior to changes in the waiting time requirements of the task that otherwise would have passed unnoticed to the rats.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral data

claim: Adult rats improved their reward rate by waiting the least possible time between trials.
source: Altogether, the data show that adult rats improved their reward rate by waiting the least possible time between trials.
evidence: Authors' summary of behavioral findings

claim: Premature execution of the learned behavioral response was more common late in training than early in training.
source: Noteworthy, premature execution of the learned behavioral response was (relatively) more common late in training than early in training, suggesting that with training behavior became less sensitive to the absence of the reward-predictive visual cue.
evidence: Behavioral observation and authors' interpretation

claim: With training behavior became less sensitive to the absence of the reward-predictive visual cue.
source: suggesting that with training behavior became less sensitive to the absence of the reward-predictive visual cue.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral data

claim: Approximately 50% of the recorded units showed higher activity preceding port entry, at the time of port exit, or both.
source: Overall, ~50% of the recorded units (473 out of 867) showed higher activity (>1 SD over baseline) preceding port entry ('anticipatory activity'; 19%, Figure 3D), at the time of port exit (18%, Figure 3E) or both before port entry and at port exit (12%, Figure 3F).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figures

claim: Neurons showing activity at task boundaries showed lower than baseline firing rates during the execution of the learned action sequence.
source: On average, these neurons showed lower than baseline firing rates during the execution of the learned action sequence (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figures

claim: There were neurons (12% of all recorded neurons) showing higher activity when the animal was inside the port than during the waiting period or at the initiation and finalization of the action sequence.
source: There were also neurons (n = 108, 12% of all recorded neurons) showing higher activity when the animal was inside the port than during the waiting period or at the initiation and finalization of the action sequence (Figure 3G).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: All main types of task-related activity emerged early during training.
source: All main types of task-related activity emerged early during training (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: The concentration of striatal activity at the beginning and end of a learned task is widely expressed in the dorsal striatum even after skilled performance is reached.
source: Overall, our data show that the concentration of striatal activity at the beginning and end of a learned task is widely expressed in the dorsal striatum even after skilled performance is reached, as reported in a recent study with a different task (Vandaele et al., 2019)⁠
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their findings in context of prior research

claim: Boundary activity is more flexible regarding the properties of the behavioral response it bounds, and carries information about its pertinent timing.
source: and suggest that, this activity is more flexible regarding the properties of the behavioral response it bounds, and carries information about its pertinent timing.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their findings

claim: The average firing rate modulation anticipating trial initiation was higher for timely than for premature trials irrespective of the upcoming action including the 8-lick sequence or not.
source: When all port entry responsive neurons were considered (i.e., port entry only plus port entry/port exit neurons), the average firing rate modulation anticipating trial initiation was higher for timely than for premature trials irrespective of the upcoming action including the 8-lick sequence or not (Figure 4A, B, F(1, 330) = 30.84, p = 7.01 × 10−8, significant main effect of trial initiation timing, no effect of action sequence-structure F(1, 330) = 0.089, p = 0.765, no interaction, F(1, 330) = 9.64 × 10−5, p = 0.992, two-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figures

claim: Anticipatory activity began 1 s before and peaked 0.5 s before the animal crossed the infrared beam located at port entry, both in premature and timely trials.
source: On average, this activity began 1 s before and peaked 0.5 s before the animal crossed the infrared beam located at port entry, both in premature and timely trials (Figure 4A).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: Accelerometer recordings did not show differences in movement initiation time between premature and timely 8-lick trials.
source: The accelerometer recordings did not show differences in movement initiation time between premature and timely 8-lick trials (0.357 ± 0.027 and 0.382 ± 0.023 s before port entry– mean and standard error of the mean (SEM) – for premature and timely trials, respectively, t(8) = 0.636, p = 0.543, Paired t-test; Figure 4C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of accelerometer data with reference to figure

claim: The 8-lick sequences emitted during premature and timely trials lasted the same and had the same latency and inter-lick interval regularity.
source: Furthermore, the 8-lick sequences emitted during premature and timely trials lasted the same and had the same latency and inter-lick interval regularity (Figure 2C–E), suggesting similar action vigor during premature and timely 8-lick trials.
evidence: Behavioral observation with reference to figures and authors' interpretation

claim: The firing rate modulation preceding trial initiation discriminates between premature and timely trials and does not predict the speed, regularity, structure, value, or vigor of the subsequently released action sequence.
source: Thus, although head acceleration data may not include differences in movements of other body parts, our data support that in this task, the firing rate modulation preceding trial initiation discriminates between premature and timely trials and does not predict the speed, regularity, structure, value, or vigor of the subsequently released action sequence.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their findings

claim: Anticipatory activity increased with a steep slope as time waited reached the learned waiting interval and then plateaued.
source: To further investigate this anticipatory activity, we plotted its amplitude at increasing waiting times observing that it increased with a steep slope as time waited reached the learned waiting interval and then plateaued (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figures

claim: There was no modulation of anticipatory neuronal activity by time waited in the following trial.
source: In contrast, there was no modulation of this neuronal activity by time waited in the following trial (Figure 4F)
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: There was no modulation of port exit-related activity by the previous waiting time.
source: nor of port exit-related activity by the previous waiting time (Figure 4G).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: The neuronal activity does not linearly report elapsed time but is rather related to changes in reward anticipation as waiting progressed.
source: The steep slope of the curve at the criterion waiting time suggested that the neuronal activity does not linearly report elapsed time but is rather related to changes in reward anticipation as waiting progressed.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of neurophysiological data

claim: In the modified task with a 5-s cutoff, the firing rate modulation preceding trial initiation increased with a steep slope at 2.5 s, but decreased after surpassing the 5-s cutoff time.
source: The firing rate modulation preceding trial initiation increased with a steep slope at 2.5 s, but instead of plateauing, it decreased after surpassing the 5-s cutoff time (Figure 4J).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: A comparison of the effects of waiting time on anticipatory activity in the tasks with and without the 5-s cutoff yielded a significant interaction.
source: A comparison of the effects of waiting time on anticipatory activity in the tasks with and without the 5-s cutoff yielded a significant interaction in a two-way RM ANOVA (Figure 4K, significant effect of task, F(1, 334) = 4.54, p = 0.034; trials, F(1.96, 656.34) = 67.73, p = 1.01 × 10−15; interaction F(2, 668) = 29.27, p = 6.53 × 10−13, two-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: The marked modulation of striatal activity preceding trial initiation probably reflects subjective changes in reward anticipation as waiting progressed.
source: In summary, the marked modulation of striatal activity preceding trial initiation probably reflects subjective changes in reward anticipation as waiting progressed.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of neurophysiological findings

claim: A small population of neurons (3% of all recorded neurons) whose activity was modulated at the time of the visual cue showed lower activity during premature trials when the visual cue was not presented.
source: In the present task, a small population of neurons whose activity was modulated at the time of the visual cue (n = 27, 3% of all recorded neurons) showed lower activity during premature trials, when the visual cue was not presented q(26) = 6.64, p = 2.15 × 10−4 versus timely trials, Tukey post hoc test after significant one-way RM ANOVA (F(1.75, 45.49) = 17.80, p = 5.00 × 10−6) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: Neurons showing increased activity during licking did not show any modulation by trial initiation timing.
source: In contrast, neurons showing increased activity during licking did not show any modulation by trial initiation timing (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figures

claim: Lick-related neurons showed largely overlapping populations with broad activity peaks encompassing many inter-lick intervals.
source: Furthermore, when we studied the neuronal activity around the individual licks, we found largely overlapping populations of positively modulated neurons with broad activity peaks encompassing many inter-lick intervals (Figure 5B).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: Lick-related modulation lasted longer during rewarded trials than in timely unrewarded and premature 8-lick trials.
source: The lick-related modulation lasted longer during rewarded trials, where licking also persisted for longer, than in timely unrewarded (>2.5 s of waiting) and premature 8-lick trials (<2.5 s of waiting).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding

claim: Lick-related modulation showed a similar amplitude irrespective of reward delivery or omission.
source: However, it showed a similar amplitude irrespective of reward delivery or omission (Figure 5B, activity centered at the eighth lick), suggesting that these neurons were modulated by licking and not by the delivery of the reward itself.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure and authors' interpretation

claim: Approximately 15% of the neurons recorded in adult rats showed responses at the time of the 8-lick that differed between trial types.
source: Overall, ~15% of the neurons recorded in adult rats (125 out of 867) showed responses at the time of the 8-lick that differed between these trial types.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding

claim: Neurons were found that responded preferentially to reward delivery (reward-responsive neurons).
source: We found neurons that responded preferentially to: (1) reward delivery (Figure 5C, 'reward-responsive neurons')
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: Neurons were found that responded preferentially to non-rewarded conditions (no reward-responsive).
source: (2) to non-rewarded conditions (Figure 5D, 'no reward-responsive')
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: Neurons were found that responded preferentially to the absence of reward during premature 8-lick trials (expected no reward-responsive).
source: and (3) to the absence of reward during premature 8-lick trials (Figure 5E, 'expected no reward-responsive').
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: 5% of all recorded neurons showed a higher activity modulation when a reward was obtained than in either no-reward conditions.
source: More specifically, 5% of all recorded neurons (n = 49) showed a higher activity modulation when a reward was obtained than in either no-reward conditions, Figure 5F top: reward-responsive neurons, Rewarded versus Unrewarded trials, q(48) = 11.18, p = 5.77 × 10–15, Rewarded versus Premature trials, q(48) = 12.52, p = 9.82 × 10–17, Unrewarded versus Premature trials, q(48) = 4.89, p = 1.18 × 10–5, Tukey test after significant one-way RM ANOVA (F(1.27, 61.14) = 66.01, p = 2.69 × 10–11).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: 5% of the striatal neurons showed activation at the time of the no-reward outcome in timely unrewarded trials and were unresponsive to reward delivery.
source: Five percent of the striatal neurons showed activation at the time of the no-reward outcome in timely unrewarded trials and were unresponsive to reward delivery (Figure 5D).
evidence: Neurophysiological finding with reference to figure

claim: No-reward-responsive neurons showed a marked activation at the time of the eighth lick during premature 8-lick trials.
source: In addition, these neurons showed a marked activation at the time of the eighth lick during premature 8-lick trials (Figure 5F middle: no reward-responsive neurons, Rewarded versus Unrewarded trials, q(45) = 12.61, p = 2.23 × 10–16, Rewarded versus Premature trials q(45) = 9.77, p = 1.08 × 10–12, Unrewarded versus Premature trials q(45) = 3.85, p = 3.69 × 10–4, Tukey test after significant one-way RM ANOVA (F(1.28, 57.7) = 57.11, p = 3.75 × 10–10)).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: 33 neurons (4% of all recorded neurons) showed a twofold higher activation at the time of the eighth lick in premature trials than in timely unrewarded trials.
source: Strikingly, there were 33 neurons (4% of all recorded neurons) that showed a twofold higher activation at the time of the eighth lick in premature trials than in timely unrewarded trials (Figure 5F bottom: Rewarded versus Unrewarded trials q(30) = 5.51, p = 5.39 × 10–6, Rewarded versus Premature trials q(30) = 12.07, p = 4.81 × 10–13, Unrewarded versus Premature trials q(30) = 10.72, p = 8.86 × 10–12, Tukey test after significant one-way RM ANOVA (F(1.71, 51.39) = 51.34, p = 2.99 × 10–9)).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: Neurons showing a higher activation during premature trials discriminated better between the two no-reward conditions.
source: However, those neurons showing a higher activation during premature trials discriminated better between the two no-reward conditions (Rewarded vs. Unrewarded trials q(45) = 0.39, p = 0.694; Rewarded vs. Premature trials q(30) = 5.01, p = 2.23 × 10–5; Unrewarded vs. Premature trials q(30) = 5.43, p = 6.89 × 10–6; mixed-effects analysis after significant one-way RM ANOVA (F(1.62, 99.89) = 11.80, p = 8.65 × 10–4), Figure 5G).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: Activity at the time of expected trial outcome reflects differences in reward prediction between premature and timely trials.
source: Overall, the data support that activity at the time of expected trial outcome reflects differences in reward prediction between premature and timely trials.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of neurophysiological findings

claim: When all port exit neurons were considered, a higher activity was observed for 8-lick trials than for trials with an incomplete licking sequence, independently of whether the trials were timely initiated or not.
source: However, when all port exit neurons were considered (i.e., port exit only plus port entry/port exit neurons), a higher activity was observed for 8-lick trials than for trials with an incomplete licking sequence, independently of whether the trials were timely initiated or not (Figure 6A, B; F(1, 101) = 36.28, p = 2.79 × 10–8 for lick sequence structure, no effect of trial timing F(1, 101) = 1.86, p = 0.176, interaction F(1, 101) = 4.07, p = 0.046, two-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figures

claim: There was no difference between trial types in the accelerometer data at the time animals exited the port.
source: Moreover, there was no difference between trial types in the accelerometer data at the time animals exited the port (Figure 6C).
evidence: Accelerometer data with reference to figure

claim: Port exit-related activity seems to tell if the learned response was emitted or not regardless of its timing and outcome.
source: Thus, port exit-related activity seems to tell if the learned response was emitted or not regardless of its timing and outcome.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of neurophysiological findings

claim: Adolescent rats successfully improved their performance in the task as shown by a higher percentage of correct trials and a higher reward rate.
source: The rats successfully improved their performance in the task as shown by a higher percentage of correct trials (Figure 7A), a higher reward rate (Figure 7B, p = 2.00 × 10–6, Wilcoxon matched pairs signed-rank test n pairs = 20)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figures

claim: Trial duration, latency to first lick and 8-lick sequence duration did not differ between 8-lick trials of adolescent and adult rats.
source: Trial duration, latency to first lick and 8-lick sequence duration did not differ between 8-lick trials of adolescent and adult rats (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: Behavioral comparison with reference to figures

claim: Accelerometer recordings from adolescent rats did not show differences of movement initiation time between premature and timely 8-lick trials.
source: Accelerometer recordings of head movements available from two adolescent rats did not show differences of movement initiation time between premature and timely 8-lick trials (0.591 ± 0.014 and 0.637 ± 0.022 mean and SEM – seconds for premature and timely trials, respectively, t(9) = 1.537, p = 0.1586, Paired t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Statistical analysis of accelerometer data with reference to figure

claim: The proportion of premature 8-lick sequence trials increased with training in adolescent rats.
source: Finally, the proportion of premature 8-lick sequence trials increased with training in adolescent rats (Figure 7C; significant effects of learning stage (F(1, 19) = 93.97, p = 8.66 × 10–9) and trial timing (F(1, 19) = 211.67, p = 9.40 × 10–12), no interaction (F(1, 19) = 5.01, p = 0.037), two-way RM ANOVA)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figure

claim: Adolescent rats released the learned action sequence prematurely more frequently than adult rats.
source: In summary, adolescent rats also released the learned action sequence prematurely despite extensive training, and indeed, they did it more frequently than adult rats (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: Behavioral comparison with reference to figures

claim: The number of premature trials per reward obtained was twofold higher in adolescent than adult rats even after training.
source: The number of premature trials per reward obtained was twofold higher in adolescent than adult rats even after training (Figure 7F; significant effects of age group (F(1, 34) = 28.51, p = 6.22 × 10–6), training (F(1, 34) = 50.19, p = 3.49 × 10–8), and interaction (F(1, 34) = 10.43, p = 2.74 × 10–3), two-way RM ANOVA)
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with reference to figure

claim: Adolescent rats achieved the same reward rate as adult rats but at the expense of a higher cost as evidenced by the excess of premature responses per reward obtained.
source: Altogether, adolescent rats achieved the same reward rate as adult rats but at the expense of a higher cost as evidenced by the excess of premature responses per reward obtained.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral findings

claim: Task-related striatal activity was qualitatively similar in adolescent and adult rats.
source: Overall, task-related striatal activity was qualitatively similar in adolescent and adult rats (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Neurophysiological comparison with reference to figure

claim: The proportion of neurons showing port entry-, port exit-, and lick-related activity was similar in adolescent and adult rats.
source: Of the registered units in adolescent rats trained in the 2.5-s waiting interval task (n = 876), the proportion of neurons showing port entry-, port exit-, and lick-related activity was similar to that found in adult rats (Figure 7H; chi-square(4) = 1.87, p = 0.759, chi-square test).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: In adolescent rats, the activations preceding port entry were higher for timely than for premature trials regardless of whether the 8-lick sequence was completed or not.
source: Also like in adult rats, the activations preceding port entry were higher for timely than for premature trials regardless of whether the 8-lick sequence was completed or not (Figure 7I, J; significant main effect of trial initiation timing F(1, 362) = 148, p = 3.72 × 10–27, no effect of action sequence structure, F(1, 362) = 1.04, p = 0.309, no interaction F(1, 362) = 0.12, p = 0.723, Two-way RM ANOVA).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figures

claim: Activations at the time of expected reward did not differ between adolescent and adult rats.
source: Activations at the time of expected reward (Figure 7K, effect on trial initiation timing (F(1.95, 76.18) = 8.53, p = 4.64 × 10−3), no effect of age (F(1, 50) = 0.42, p = 0.518), no interaction (F(2, 78) = 0.95, p = 0.390), Restricted Maximum Likelihood [REML] test)
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: Activity at port exit did not differ between adolescent and adult rats.
source: and activity at port exit – probably reflecting that the correct action sequence was emitted (Figure 7L, sequence structure, F(1, 356) = 124.14, p = 6.18 × 10−25, timing F(1, 356) = 4.11, p = 0.043, significant interaction between trial initiation timing and sequence structure F(1, 356) = 21.21, p = 5.74 × 10–6, three-way ANOVA), did not differ between adolescent and adult rats (effect of age F(1, 356) = 0.12, p = 0.727).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data with reference to figure

claim: The amplitude modulation of striatal activity preceding trial initiations at increasing waiting times differed between adolescent and adult rats.
source: On the other hand, the data displaying the amplitude modulation of striatal activity preceding trial initiations at increasing waiting times (n = 235 and 124 striatal neurons for adolescent and adult rats, respectively) differed between adolescent and adult rats (Figure 7M).
evidence: Neurophysiological comparison with reference to figure

claim: The adolescent rats curve showed a significantly steeper increase than the adult rats curve in the modulation of anticipatory activity.
source: Importantly, the adolescent rats curve showed a significantly steeper increase than the adult rats curve (p2 coefficient of the logistic function, profile likelihood estimation of the 95% confidence interval: adolescent rats = 1.080 (95% CI: 0.533–2.160) and adult rats = 0.4525 (95% CI: 0.273–0.747); F(1, 16) = 4.86, p = 0.042).
evidence: Statistical analysis of neurophysiological data

claim: The curve of the adolescent group showed a significantly steeper growth rate in the cumulative frequency distribution of 8-lick trial initiation times.
source: As expected, the curve of the adolescent group showed a significantly steeper growth rate (p2 coefficient of the logistic function, profile likelihood estimation of 95% confidence interval: adolescent rats = 0.703 (95% CI: 0.683–0.724) and adult rats = 0.392 (95% CI: 0.380–0.406), F(1, 9960)=658.8, p = 9.60 × 10–14).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: Adolescent rats showed relatively more timely trials than adult rats at short times after the criterion wait time was surpassed.
source: Remarkably, in addition to a relative excess of premature 8-lick trials, the adolescent rats showed relatively more timely trials than adult rats at short times after the criterion wait time was surpassed (Figure 7N), suggesting that adult rats are more tolerant to reward delay.
evidence: Behavioral observation with reference to figure and authors' interpretation

claim: Adult rats are more tolerant to reward delay than adolescent rats.
source: suggesting that adult rats are more tolerant to reward delay.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral data

claim: There was a significant correlation between the p2 parameters obtained for the waiting modulation of neuronal activity and trial initiation times.
source: Finally, we adjusted the logistic function to the data of each rat separately. We then computed a correlation between the p2 parameters obtained for the waiting modulation of neuronal activity and trial initiation times, and found a significant correlation (Figure 7O, R2 = 0.833, p = 2 × 10–4, n = 10).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reference to figure

claim: The waiting modulation of reward anticipation grows with a steeper slope in adolescent rats, likely reflecting age-related changes in temporal discounting, internal urgency states or explore–exploit balance.
source: In sum, the data show that the waiting modulation of reward anticipation grows at a faster rate in adolescent rats, paralleling a higher rate of accumulation of initiated trials across time in this age group.
evidence: Authors' summary and interpretation of findings

claim: The present task resembles differential reinforcement of low rates of responding protocols (DRL) that are used to assess response inhibition and timing factors associated with impulsivity.
source: The task resembles differential reinforcement of low rates of responding protocols (DRL) that are used to assess response inhibition and timing factors associated with impulsivity (Monterosso and Ainslie, 1999; Neill, 1976)⁠.
evidence: Comparison to established methods with citations

claim: Factors that increase premature responding in humans also increase premature responding in rodents trained with DRL procedures.
source: Factors that increase premature responding in humans, such as psychostimulant drugs (Evenden, 1998)⁠, psychostimulant withdrawal (Peterson et al., 2003)⁠, D2-type receptor agonists (Engeln et al., 2016)⁠, maternal separation and social isolation (Lovic et al., 2011)⁠, sleep restriction (Kamphuis et al., 2017),⁠ and adolescence (Andrzejewski et al., 2011)⁠ also increase premature responding in rodents trained with DRL procedures.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: DRL procedures have been used in educational and clinically meaningful contexts to reduce impulsive behavior.
source: Furthermore, these procedures have been used in educational and clinically meaningful contexts to reduce impulsive behavior (Bonner and Borrero, 2018; Lennox et al., 1987)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The present task requires responding with an action sequence that becomes highly automatized with training and could not always be stopped despite sensory feedback telling that it will not be rewarded.
source: Unlike classical DRL procedures, the present task requires responding with an action sequence that becomes highly automatized with training and could not always be stopped despite sensory feedback telling that it will not be rewarded.
evidence: Description of task characteristics

claim: The premature releases of the learned action sequence are necessary to learn the duration of the waiting interval and to adapt to its changes.
source: Interestingly, although premature responding showed an overall decrease with training, the premature releases of the learned action sequence were selectively preserved, suggesting that these responses are necessary to learn the duration of the waiting interval and to adapt to its changes.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral findings

claim: Adolescent rats learn the task but make more premature responses per reward obtained.
source: Importantly, adolescent rats learn the task but make more premature responses per reward obtained.
evidence: Behavioral finding

claim: Adolescent rats initiate their timely trials closer to the criterion wait time than the adult rats, supporting that they are less patient.
source: In addition, they initiate their timely trials closer to the criterion wait time than the adult rats, supporting that they are less patient.
evidence: Behavioral finding and authors' interpretation

claim: The adolescent rats take a higher risk of releasing the learned action sequence prematurely, which makes them more impulsive than adult rats in the present task.
source: Overall, the adolescent rats seem to take a higher risk of releasing the learned action sequence prematurely, which makes them more impulsive than adult rats in the present task.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral findings

claim: Recent studies link premature responding in anticipation of reinforcement to a higher tendency to automatize behavior and form habits.
source: Recent studies link premature responding in anticipation of reinforcement to a higher tendency to automatize behavior and form habits (Everitt et al., 2008; Voon et al., 2015)⁠⁠.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent research

claim: Striatal activity marking the boundaries of automatized action chains has been perceived as a sign of 'packaged behavioral sequences' that would be difficult to stop after their release.
source: Striatal activity marking the boundaries of automatized action chains has been perceived as a sign of 'packaged behavioral sequences' (Graybiel, 2008)⁠ that would be difficult to stop after their release regardless of whether their initiation was more or less goal directed (Geddes et al., 2018; Robbins and Costa, 2017)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The representation of task events contributing to goal-directed behavior persists in the DMS even after extensive training.
source: While this 'bracketing activity' prevails in the DLS, according to some studies, the representation of task events contributing to goal-directed behavior persists in the DMS even after extensive training (Kubota et al., 2009; Thorn et al., 2010)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Parallel representations in DLS and DMS may allow switching between automatic and deliberation-based task-solving strategies when outcomes change.
source: These parallel representations may allow switching between automatic and deliberation-based task-solving strategies when outcomes change (Balleine and Dickinson, 1998; Daw et al., 2005; Yin and Knowlton, 2006)⁠
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: A stronger boundary activity and/or a less precise coding of task events could explain the higher rates of premature responding observed in adolescent rats.
source: The remarkably similar behavior observed in 8-lick prematurely released and timely unrewarded trials led us to expect that a stronger boundary activity, and/or a less precise coding of task events, could explain the higher rates of premature responding observed in adolescent rats.
evidence: Authors' hypothesis based on their observations

claim: A recent study suggested that the stronger the activity at the action initiation, the lower the deliberation at the turn-choice site in a T-maze task.
source: Indeed, a recent study suggested that the stronger the activity at the action initiation, the lower the deliberation at the turn-choice site in a T-maze task (Smith and Graybiel, 2013)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The strength of anticipatory activity increased with the time waited before response release and was higher in the more impulsive adolescent rats.
source: Here, the strength of anticipatory activity increased with the time waited before response release and was higher in the more impulsive adolescent rats.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding from the study

claim: Anticipatory activity did not predict that the rewarded 8-lick sequence would be included in the behavioral response.
source: However, it did not predict that the rewarded 8-lick sequence would be included in the behavioral response.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding from the study

claim: A similar activity followed all responses containing the learned 8-lick sequence regardless of trial outcome.
source: On the other hand, a similar activity followed all responses containing the learned 8-lick sequence regardless of trial outcome and despite the markedly different lick rates observed between rewarded and unrewarded responses after outcome disclosure.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding from the study

claim: Hierarchical control during action sequence execution may allow the selective removal of intermediate sequence elements.
source: A recent study showed that hierarchical control during action sequence execution may allow the selective removal of intermediate sequence elements (Geddes et al., 2018)⁠
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The activity of many striatal neurons seemed to continuously follow the expression of the lick sequence.
source: Importantly, the activity of many striatal neurons seemed to continuously follow the expression of the lick sequence as has also been reported previously by others (Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin et al., 2014; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015)⁠
evidence: Neurophysiological finding supported by citations to prior research

claim: A recent study showed a continuous modulation of striatal neuronal activity across the initiation, execution, and termination of cue-guided locomotion.
source: and a recent study showed a continuous modulation of striatal neuronal activity across the initiation, execution, and termination of cue-guided locomotion (Sales-Carbonell et al., 2018)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent research

claim: Striatal activity is more flexible regarding the properties of the behavioral response it bounds, and carries information about its pertinent timing.
source: and suggest that, this activity is more flexible regarding the properties of the behavioral response it bounds, and carries information about its pertinent timing.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their findings

claim: Striatal signals at the time of expected outcome discriminated between rewarded and unrewarded correct trials.
source: Striatal signals at the time of expected outcome not only discriminated between rewarded and unrewarded correct trials as observed by others (Atallah et al., 2014; Nonomura et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2018)⁠
evidence: Neurophysiological finding supported by citations to prior research

claim: A specific outcome evaluation signal after premature 8-lick trials may serve to inhibit premature responding and minimize the exploration of the waiting interval.
source: A specific outcome evaluation signal after premature 8-lick trials may serve to inhibit premature responding and minimize the exploration of the waiting interval.

claim: To compute an outcome signal, the animal has to retain information regarding the time waited before responding while monitoring the execution of the lick sequence.
source: To compute such outcome signal, the animal has to retain information regarding the time waited before responding (or regarding visual feedback on proper trial initiation timing) while monitoring the execution of the lick sequence.
evidence: Authors' reasoning about computational requirements

claim: Information about trial initiation timing or the visual cue should arrive at outcome-sensitive ensembles through mechanisms likely involving inputs from prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex areas.
source: Thus, the sustained lick-related signal may serve to estimate outcome timing (Zold and Hussain Shuler, 2015)⁠, but information about trial initiation timing or the visual cue should arrive at outcome-sensitive ensembles through other mechanisms likely involving inputs from prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex areas (Asaad et al., 2017; Hamid et al., 2021; Wassum et al., 2011).
evidence: Authors' interpretation supported by citations to prior research

claim: No differences in outcome evaluation signals were found that could explain the more impulsive behavior of adolescent rats.
source: Nonetheless, we found no differences in outcome evaluation signals that could explain the more impulsive behavior of adolescent rats.
evidence: Neurophysiological finding from the study

claim: Premature responding has classically been linked to poor behavioral inhibition.
source: On the other hand, although premature responding has classically been linked to poor behavioral inhibition (Bari and Robbins, 2013)⁠
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

source: alternative views equates it to preferring a smaller more immediate reward over a larger delayed one (Dalley and Robbins, 2017; Monterosso and Ainslie, 1999)⁠
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

source: and to deficient gathering or evaluation of evidence while waiting (Dalley and Robbins, 2017)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

source: Interestingly, influential models propose that time estimates derived from accumulation of pacemaker counts can be compared to a memorized time interval to decide whether a target time has been reached or not (Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Gibbon, 1977; Namboodiri and Hussain Shuler, 2016)⁠.

claim: Previous studies showed that dorsal striatum ensembles can provide time estimations.
source: Previous studies showed that dorsal striatum ensembles can provide time estimations (Bakhurin et al., 2017; Emmons et al., 2017; Gouvêa et al., 2015; Matell et al., 2003; Mello et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2020)

source: and we also found sequential and tonic ensemble activation during the waiting period (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) that could serve to track time while waiting in the present task.

claim: By comparing the time accumulated while waiting against the memorized waiting interval, the animal could anticipate how likely is the upcoming action to be rewarded.
source: By comparing the time accumulated while waiting against the memorized waiting interval, the animal could anticipate how likely is the upcoming action to be rewarded.

source: How fast reward expectancy steps up when time waited approaches the reference time interval would depend on several factors, including temporal discounting effects on reward value (Monterosso and Ainslie, 1999; Namboodiri and Hussain Shuler, 2016; Wittmann and Paulus, 2008)⁠.
evidence: Authors' reasoning supported by citations to prior research

claim: The anticipatory signal could be interpreted as a reading of the temporal discount function at the time chosen to release the learned action sequence.
source: In this sense, the anticipatory signal we observe could be interpreted as a reading of the temporal discount function at the time chosen to release the learned action sequence.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their findings

claim: According to a recent theory, animals time their decisions by estimating if they can improve the reward rate experienced in the recent past.
source: A recent theory proposes that animals time their decisions by estimating if they can improve the reward rate experienced in the recent past; according to it, the longer the time window over which reinforcement history is estimated, the higher the tolerance to delays of future rewards (i.e., the less steep the temporal discount effect) (Namboodiri et al., 2014)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent theory

claim: Adults should be able to integrate information about past reinforcement history over longer time windows than adolescents.
source: Adults should be able to integrate information about past reinforcement history over longer time windows that adolescents (Namboodiri et al., 2014)⁠
evidence: Inference supported by citation to prior research

claim: Temporal discount rate decreases throughout childhood and adolescence.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Alternative theories propose that waiting impulsivity relates to perceiving durations longer than they are, which would be associated to perceiving a higher cost of time and with a steeper temporal discounting.
source: Alternative theories propose that waiting impulsivity relates to perceiving durations longer than they are, which would be associated to perceiving a higher cost of time and with a steeper temporal discounting (Wittmann and Paulus, 2008)⁠.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Time perception depends on several cognitive processes that are modified by adolescence including working memory, attention, and mood.
source: Moreover, time perception depends on several cognitive processes that are modified by adolescence including working memory, attention, and mood (Baumann and Odum, 2012; Wittmann and Paulus, 2008)⁠.

claim: Adolescent rats achieve a similar reward rate to adult rats and do not show the negative effect of premature trials on reward rate that is observed in adults.
source: Interestingly, in the present task, adolescent rats achieve a similar reward rate to adult rats and, indeed, they do not show the negative effect of premature trials on reward rate that is observed in adults (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: By prematurely executing the learned action sequence, adolescents would likely get more precise information regarding the duration of the waiting interval.
source: Importantly, although they achieve this reward rate at the expense of a higher energy cost (more premature trials per reward obtained), by prematurely executing the learned action sequence, adolescents would likely get more precise information regarding the duration of the waiting interval, which, in turn, would refresh more frequently their cognitive map of the task.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of behavioral findings

claim: Impulsivity is advantageous when it helps to adapt to uncertain environments.
source: This view is consistent with the idea that impulsivity is advantageous when it helps to adapt to uncertain environments and that increased exploratory behavior in adolescence allows gaining knowledge that would be useful to guide decisions in adulthood (Addicott et al., 2017; Spear, 2000)⁠.

claim: Increased exploratory behavior in adolescence allows gaining knowledge that would be useful to guide decisions in adulthood.
